Restart the PostgreSQL server
Connect as the superuser (e.g. `psql -U postgres`) and reset the password with `ALTER USER <name> WITH PASSWORD '<new>'`
Restore the original pg_hba.conf and restart again, because leaving trust authentication is very dangerous

question: My transaction dies with 'ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update'. Why does it happen and what should the application do?

evidence.quote: ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
applications using these levels must be prepared to retry transactions that fail due to serialization errors

key_points.text: It happens at Repeatable Read (snapshot isolation): another concurrent transaction updated or deleted a row this transaction wants to modify and committed, so this one is rolled back
The application should abort the transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning (it will then see the committed change)
The error has SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure); PostgreSQL has no automatic retry, so the retry must include all logic that decides which SQL/values to use

verify_note: | key_points added before the Phase 5 holdout run, written and checked by the assistant against the source text: Read transaction-iso.html (the error text, why, 'abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction') and mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html (SQLSTATE 40001, retry the complete transaction, no automatic retry).

question: ERROR: canceling statement due to conflict with recovery. My long report query on the standby keeps getting killed. How do I stop that?

evidence.quote: has to forcibly cancel all queries which can use these rows

key_points.text: Cause: the primary's VACUUM removes old row versions that the standby query still needs, so the standby cancels the query

Stop the cancellations with at least one of: set hot_standby_feedback on the standby, raise max_standby_streaming_delay, or keep a repeatable read transaction open on the primary so old row versions are not vacuumed
Trade-off: hot_standby_feedback or a held transaction delays cleanup of dead rows on the primary (table bloat)

verify_note: Read the SO accepted answer (dummy repeatable read transaction) and postgres/hot-standby.html conflict section (hot_standby_feedback, max_standby_*_delay). Fix point merges these documented alternatives.

question: Replica lag keeps growing on my PostgreSQL standby. How do I tell whether the primary, the network or the standby is the bottleneck?

evidence.quote: might indicate network delay, or that the standby is under heavy load

key_points.text: Compare pg_current_wal_lsn on the primary with the sent_lsn field of pg_stat_replication: a large difference means the primary is under heavy load
Compare sent_lsn with pg_last_wal_receive_lsn on the standby: a large difference means network delay or a standby under heavy load
On a hot standby, a large difference between pg_last_wal_replay_lsn and flushed_lsn in pg_stat_wal_receiver means WAL is received faster than it is replayed

verify_note: Read warm-standby.html 26.2.5.2 Monitoring: all three comparisons are stated; the first two answer primary/network/standby.

question: Our PostgreSQL tables keep taking more disk space even though we regularly delete lots of rows. What is going on?

evidence.quote: moderately-frequent standard `VACUUM` runs are a better approach than infrequent `VACUUM FULL` runs

key_points.text: UPDATE or DELETE does not remove the old row version immediately (MVCC); dead row versions stay until VACUUM cleans them up

Standard VACUUM only marks the space reusable and does not return it to the operating system; VACUUM FULL compacts the table and returns space, but needs an exclusive lock and extra disk space while it runs
Run standard VACUUM often enough (autovacuum does this and never issues VACUUM FULL); do not disable autovacuum

verify_note: Read routine-vacuuming 24.1.2 Recovering Disk Space in full. Points 1-2 are the explanation the question asks for; routine-vacuum advice optional.

question: Pods keep getting evicted from one node that is running low on memory and disk. How does that work and how do I tune it?

evidence.quote: ## Eviction signals and thresholds

key_points.text: The kubelet compares eviction signals (e.g. memory.available, nodefs.available, imagefs.available) with eviction thresholds, the minimum amount of the resource that should be available on the node, and evicts Pods when a threshold is met

Tune it by setting eviction thresholds on the kubelet: soft thresholds (eviction-soft with eviction-soft-grace-period, optionally eviction-max-pod-grace-period) or hard thresholds (eviction-hard, no grace period), written like memory.available<1Gi or as percentages
Default hard thresholds include memory.available<100Mi, nodefs.available<10% and imagefs.available<15%; changing one parameter resets the others to 0 unless all are given

question: I run PostgreSQL on Kubernetes. How do I keep the data across pod restarts and also archive WAL for point-in-time recovery?

evidence.quote: have a lifecycle independent of any individual Pod that uses the PV
# 25.3. Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)

key_points.text: Kubernetes: keep the data directory on a PersistentVolume claimed through a PersistentVolumeClaim, whose lifecycle is independent of any individual Pod, so data survives pod restarts
PostgreSQL: combine a file-system-level base backup with continuously archived WAL files; this supports point-in-time recovery to any time since the base backup
Enable WAL archiving by setting wal_level to replica or higher, archive_mode to on, and an archive_command (or archive_library) that copies finished WAL segments; pg_dump cannot be used for this

verify_note: Read persistent-volumes Introduction (PV/PVC lifecycle independent of Pod) and continuous-archiving 25.3 and 25.3.1 (base backup + WAL, archive_mode/archive_command). One point per product, both essential.

key_points.text: Re-checkout and pull the branch in the workflow with `git checkout "${GITHUB_REF:11}" && git pull` so lerna finds the branch

Point the origin remote at a URL with a personal access token (`git remote set-url origin https://$GITHUB_ACTOR:$GITHUB_PAT@github.com/<owner>/<repo>`, token from repository secrets) so lerna can push tags and commits
Run `npm whoami` after setting up auth, so a broken authentication is caught before lerna publish pushes tags

verify_note: Read the SO question and the updated accepted answer (list of key features); the draft key points were a subset. Which feature fixes the branch error is the answerer's reading: re-checkout and pull is the direct one.

question: My Kafka Streams application stops with an exception from FailOnInvalidTimestamp because a record has a negative timestamp. How can I keep it running?

evidence.quote: If you have data with invalid timestamps and want to process it, then there are two alternative extractors available.

key_points.text: Use another timestamp extractor, at least one of: LogAndSkipOnInvalidTimestamp (logs a warning and drops the record so Streams can make progress) or UsePartitionTimeOnInvalidTimestamp (uses the previous valid timestamp of the same partition as an estimate, and throws if none exists)
WallclockTimestampExtractor returns the current system time instead of extracting a timestamp

verify_note: Read config-streams.md timestamp-extractor quote block: both alternative extractors and the wall-clock one described.

question: Evicting a pod through the Eviction API returns '429 Too Many Requests'. What does that mean and what can I do?

evidence.quote: the eviction is not currently allowed because of the configured pod-disruption-budget.

key_points.text: The eviction is not currently allowed because of the configured PodDisruptionBudget; you may be able to attempt the eviction again later
The same response can also come from API rate limiting

verify_note: Read api-eviction.md response list (200, 429, 500): sentence verbatim.

question: My GitHub Actions job that deploys over SSH fails with 'Permission denied (publickey,gssapi-keyex,gssapi-with-mic)'. How do I set up the key and known hosts?

evidence.quote: Apparently keys were protected with passphrase

key_points.text: The keys were protected with a passphrase: generate a new key pair without one (`ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -N ""`) and add the public key to the server's authorized_keys (ssh-copy-id)
Store the private key and the server's known_hosts entry (from ssh-keyscan) as GitHub secrets and write them to files in the workflow step (chmod 600 on the key), then connect with ssh -i

verify_note: Read the SO question (workflow with key and known_hosts from secrets) and accepted answer (steps 1-5 plus workflow).
